title: Biological agents and exposure boundaries
audience: Cleaners working near laboratories where biological agents may be present.
learningOutcomes: Explain why biological agents are outside a cleaner's authority.
Recognise the signs that biological material may be present, and keep clear.
Stop, record and refer any exposure concern or unidentified material.

instruction.heading: What counts as a biological agent in a laboratory
instruction.body: In a laboratory, a biological agent is any living or once-living material that could cause disease or harm if people were exposed to it. The group includes bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and some toxins produced by living things. A sample tube, a culture plate, a waste container, a centrifuge, a freezer, or a spill on a bench may each contain material of this kind, and nothing about the outside of the item tells you what is inside. For a cleaner, the practical point is simple. You cannot tell by looking whether a material is safe, and the people who can tell are the laboratory staff who know the agent, the containment and the procedure for it. This is why the work of identifying, sampling, containing and decontaminating biological material belongs to trained laboratory personnel working under the laboratory's own documented methods. A cleaner's role is to recognise that the material may be there, keep clear, and pass the matter on.

instruction.heading: Why this sits outside routine cleaning
instruction.body: Routine housekeeping assumes that the surfaces and items in the room are ordinary. A laboratory cannot make that assumption. Wiping a bench that has a biological spill on it spreads the material, and so does lifting a lid, moving a rack or sweeping a floor where containers have been dropped. The Commonwealth security sensitive biological agents scheme covers entities and facilities that handle suspected or known security sensitive biological agents in Australia, and it sets registration duties for those who handle these agents on an ongoing basis. The list of agents is set by the Minister for Health and Aged Care and is not published on the scheme page, so a cleaner cannot tell from the scheme alone whether a particular material is listed. Nothing in this lesson gives a cleaner any role under the scheme, and a cleaner working to this lesson does not handle these agents. Whatever the laboratory's own registration and procedures are, the cleaner's job is to stay out of that work.

instruction.heading: Signs that material may be present, and keeping clear
instruction.body: Signs that biological material may be present include biohazard signage, sealed containers with a biological label, restricted-entry signs, equipment marked not to be opened, cold storage with a warning label, and an unfamiliar spill or leak on a bench or floor. Some signs are only words, and some are only a colour or symbol. Treat any sign that you do not fully understand as a reason to keep clear, and do not decide that it is out of date. Keep clear of the marked area, the area under it, and any path that would take you past it. Do not touch the material, do not pick up a container that has been dropped, and do not try to identify the content by smell, colour, or appearance. Record the location, the sign or condition, and the time, from a safe distance. If you need to note what you can see, describe it in plain words, such as a dropped tube with a label, rather than guessing what is in it.

instruction.heading: Possible exposure: stop, leave and report
instruction.body: If you may have been exposed, stop what you are doing, leave the area by the route you came in, and follow the site's emergency and exposure route. Exposure can happen through a cut or puncture, through a splash to the eyes, nose or mouth, through skin that has been in contact with the material, or through breathing an aerosol or an unfamiliar odour. Do not wait to see whether symptoms develop, and do not carry on with the job. Use the site's first aid and washing facilities as the exposure route describes, and do not attempt treatment beyond that. Report the concern to the laboratory supervisor or site contact at once, and tell them what happened, where, when, and whether you touched anything. Record the time, the location, the people informed and the first aid given, and ask for medical advice through the route the site has set. Medical follow-up is a matter for the treating clinician, and this lesson does not give any clinical instructions.

instruction.heading: Unidentified material and the refer-on rule
instruction.body: Sometimes you will find material that nobody has labelled, such as a container of unknown liquid, a plate with growth on it, or a box of small tubes left on a trolley. The rule is the same as for a labelled leak. You do not identify it, open it, move it to a cleaner place, or put it in a general bin. You record it and refer it. The record names what is visible, where it is, the time, and who you informed, and it asks the laboratory staff to make the decision about collection, containment or any further step. The refer-on rule also applies when a person asks you to help with something outside the cleaning task, such as moving samples to a fridge or taking a container to the sink. The answer is that the task is outside your authority, and the request goes back to the laboratory staff in writing. This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

instruction.heading: Worked boundary: a sealed container and a second, quieter risk
instruction.body: Imagine a corridor with a sealed container labelled as biological. The container has been left on a bench and there is a small wet mark beneath it. The cleaner's task is to tidy the bench. The correct boundary is that the bench is excluded from the cleaning until the laboratory staff have dealt with the container and the mark, and the cleaner keeps clear of both. There is a second, quieter risk in the same corridor, which is a small glass fragment on the floor near the wet mark. The fragment is not a biological item in itself, but it may have been part of a container that held one. Do not pick the fragment up, and do not wipe the mark, because wiping spreads whatever is there. Record the fragment, the mark, the container and their locations from a distance, and tell the laboratory staff. The lesson for the cleaner is that a small or ordinary-looking item in the same spot as a biological sign is treated as part of the sign, not as a separate, cleanable job.

procedure: Keep clear of areas with biohazard signage, sealed or labelled containers, restricted-entry signs, or unfamiliar spills and leaks.
Do not touch, move, sample, open or identify any biological material, including dropped containers and small items near a sign.
Record the location, the sign or condition, and the time, from a safe distance, in plain words.
If exposure is possible, stop, leave by the entry route and follow the site's emergency and exposure route, including first aid and washing facilities.
Report the concern at once to the laboratory supervisor or site contact, and record the time, location, people informed and first aid given.
Refer unidentified material to the laboratory staff in writing, and do not place it in a general bin or move it.
Do not resume the affected area until the laboratory staff have given a written, updated scope.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner sees a sealed container with a biohazard label that has leaked onto a bench. The cleaner has not touched it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and does the bench get wiped before the staff arrive?
workedExamples.reasoning: Keep clear, do not touch the leak, and leave the immediate area by the entry route. Record the location and the condition from a distance, including the time and the label as you can read it from there. Report at once to the laboratory staff. The bench is not wiped, because wiping spreads the leak. The bench is excluded until the staff have dealt with it and given a written updated scope.

workedExamples.situation: While emptying a pinned notice board, a cleaner cuts a finger on a broken glass tube that was lying behind a box. The tube held an unlabelled liquid. The cut is bleeding and the cleaner is unsure whether the liquid touched the wound.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, what is reported, and what is recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop, leave the area by the entry route, and follow the site's first aid and washing route for a cut that may be contaminated. Do not wait to see whether symptoms develop. Report the cut and the possible exposure to the laboratory supervisor at once, and say which tube it was and where it was found. Record the time, the location, the people informed and the first aid given. Ask for medical advice through the site's route. Do not clean up the glass or the liquid, and do not identify the liquid. The laboratory staff decide how the glass and liquid are managed.

workedExamples.situation: A cold storage unit in a laboratory has a warning label that you cannot fully read from the corridor. A colleague asks you to check whether the door has closed properly while you dust the corridor.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you check the door, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not check the door. The unit is a marked item in a laboratory, and checking it is outside the cleaning task and the cleaner's authority. Keep clear of the unit, record its location, the label as you can read it from the corridor, and the time, and tell the laboratory staff that the door may need checking. The colleague's request is referred to the staff in writing, and the corridor dusting continues only where the staff have confirmed the area is open.

equipmentAndPpe: Laboratory emergency and exposure route information, including the first aid and washing facilities for the area.
Contact card for the laboratory supervisor and the site emergency contact.
Deferral and exposure record form, with fields for location, time, people informed and first aid given.

Personal protective equipment as set by the site procedure for approved housekeeping tasks only. Personal protective equipment does not make entry to a biological area acceptable. Safe Work Australia describes personal protective equipment as among the least effective control measures, used after higher-level controls such as removing the hazard.
No sampling, collection or identification tools. A cleaner does not use these in a biological area.

commonErrors.error: Wiping up a leak from a biohazard container, because it looks small and the bench is in the job.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep clear and report to laboratory staff. Do not wipe, touch or move the leak.

commonErrors.error: Identifying material by smell, colour or appearance and deciding it is harmless.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not identify the material. Record what you can see in plain words and refer it to trained personnel.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring a possible exposure because no symptoms have appeared.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, leave, follow the exposure route and report at once. Do not wait to see whether symptoms develop.

commonErrors.error: Picking up a dropped tube or small item near a biohazard sign because it looks ordinary.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat small items near a sign as part of the sign. Leave them for the laboratory staff.

commonErrors.error: Checking a marked cold storage unit or door when asked by a colleague.
commonErrors.prevention: A request from a colleague does not extend the cleaner's authority. Refer it to the laboratory staff in writing.

commonErrors.error: Delaying the report to finish the job first.
commonErrors.prevention: Report the concern first. The job waits until the report has been made and the affected area has a written scope.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care describes the Security Sensitive Biological Agents scheme as covering entities and facilities that handle suspected or known security sensitive biological agents in Australia. The scheme page states that anyone who plans to handle these agents on an ongoing basis must register as an entity, and it sets a two business day window for the initial registration report. The page does not publish the agent list. A cleaner does not handle these agents under this lesson.

Work with other biological agents is controlled by the laboratory's own procedures and by state and territory requirements. This lesson does not authorise any biological work, including identification, sampling, containment, decontamination or waste handling.

Safe Work Australia describes personal protective equipment as one of the least effective control measures, to be used after higher-level controls, and places the duty to provide and train people in its use on the person conducting the business or undertaking. A site's protective equipment list does not extend a cleaner's scope into a biological area.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

qualityStandard: Biohazard area and labelled containers identified and kept clear in the simulation, with no contact by the cleaner.
Recording made from a safe distance, in plain words, with no identification of the material.
Possible exposure stopped, reported at once, and recorded with the time, location, people informed and first aid given.
Unidentified material referred to laboratory staff in writing, with no movement, sampling or disposal by the cleaner.
documentationEvidence: Location and condition record made from a safe distance, with the time and the observer.
Exposure concern and report record, with the time, location, people informed and first aid given.
Written referral of unidentified or leaking material to the laboratory staff, with the decision requested.
Written updated scope from the laboratory staff before the affected area is resumed.
summary: A cleaner does not identify, sample, contain, move or decontaminate biological material.
Keep clear of signs and labelled containers, and record from a safe distance in plain words.
If exposure is possible, stop, leave, follow the exposure route and report at once.
Refer unidentified material and any colleague request outside the task to the laboratory staff in writing.

knowledgeChecks.question: A biohazard container has leaked onto a bench. What is correct?
options: Keep clear, record from a distance, and report to laboratory staff
Wipe it up quickly so the bench is clean for the staff
Identify the material before reporting it, so the report is accurate

knowledgeChecks.question: Who identifies biological material in a laboratory?
options: The cleaner, once they have seen enough of the material to know it
Trained laboratory personnel working under the laboratory's procedures
Any visitor who has a view on it and wants to say what it is

knowledgeChecks.question: You may have been exposed to material while cleaning. What is correct?
options: Wait and see whether any symptoms develop over the next hour or two
Keep working and report at the end of the shift, once the task is done
Stop, leave by the entry route, follow the exposure route and report at once

knowledgeChecks.question: A small glass fragment lies near a biohazard sign. What should you do?
options: Pick it up because it looks ordinary and is not sharp to the touch
Treat it as part of the sign, leave it, and record its location from a distance
Sweep it into the general bin, since it is small and easy to lose from the floor
